extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded investigators, grant applicants, program officers, and others interested in NIH funding policy
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of the criteria and processes that determine which NIH grant applications get funded — the relative roles of peer review percentile scores, institute paylines, and Program/IC staff portfolio/prioritization decisions. Useful for investigators trying to understand how funding outcomes are decided and why exceptions occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program staff broader perspective / portfolio view
rubrics_metrics.description: They. Have. A. Different. Perspective. A broader perspective. In the best of all worlds, the Program Staff have the opportunity to step back and look at the larger trends within the science that is within their jurisdiction. To see where current fads have left holes in their portfolio. To perhaps take a risk where the peers are conservative. To identify the duplications and overlaps within their own portfolio and adjust accordingly. To worry about the next generation of scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program staff evaluate applications not only on scientific merit but on how they fit and balance an institute's portfolio, fill gaps left by trends, reduce duplication, support the next generation, and enable strategic risk-taking. Use this criterion to anticipate programmatic picks or declines even when peer review score is favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review priority score / percentile
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority score/percentile emerging from initial peer review is a major signal: 'There is a clear payline (formally published or not, you can see where it lies) below which almost everything gets funded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should treat percentile rank as the dominant signal for funding chances. The NIGMS data cited show funded/unfunded distributions tied to percentile; moving closer to the payline increases odds of being funded as an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payline and gray-zone (exception) funding
rubrics_metrics.description: A hard payline exists below which most applications are funded; above that is a 'grey area' where only a subset are funded as exceptions/pickups. Example: NCI reportedly had a payline in the 7-8%ile zone and 'consider' everything up to some 25%ile for exception funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand where an IC's effective payline lies. Applications well below the payline are likely funded; those in the grey zone have variable chances depending on distance from the payline and programmatic priorities. Expect explicit or implicit thresholds and occasional out-of-order pickups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review triage based on portfolio fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue that grants that do not fit the IC portfolio should not be sent forward for peer review (or for A1 revision). The commenter: 'If the grants do not fit the NCI portofolio they should not be sent forward for peer review in the first instance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic triage before peer review can save resources but risks denying specialist reviewers the chance to judge scientific fit and may remove applicants' opportunity to respond to reviews. Anticipate that programmatic pre-triage is possible but controversial; if concerned, communicate with SROs/POs before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program staff resource and information limits (not omniscient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program staff are not omniscient. 'They need their extramural scientists to educate them. Not to dictate their job priorities... To educate. To provide a portion of the knowledge, information and evidence that Program staff require to do their part of the job.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that Program decisions are informed but limited by available expertise and information. High-quality applications should 'make their case' clearly so both peer reviewers and Program staff can evaluate fit; do not assume Program will have deep technical knowledge of every area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of abstract-only triage
rubrics_metrics.description: The only realistic way heavy programmatic pre-triage would scale is by triaging on the basis of the Abstract: 'The only way that would work is if someone at the Program level does a lot of triaging on the basis of the Abstract... POs are not going to be reading all the apps in detail under such a scenario.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Program triage is likely, craft the abstract/title/specific aims to clearly communicate portfolio fit and significance; rely on the fact that abstracts may be used for quick programmatic screening, but also be aware of the risk of oversimplification and mistaken rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmatic pickups balanced against peer-review rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where programmatic exceptions occur, the priority score still strongly influences pickups: 'The chances of an application being funded as an exception to the payline increases as the score moves closer to that payline.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When targeting pickups, aim for a competitive score as programmatic exceptions are more likely for applications nearer the payline; low-ranked applications are unlikely to be rescued regardless of program interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding redundant funding / consideration of existing support
rubrics_metrics.description: Program staff may decline or deprioritize applications if the applicant already holds substantial funding or the proposed work would be redundant within the portfolio: comment example — dropped apps might be to people who already had a larger grant and concern about redundant funding was present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate distinctiveness from an applicant's current awards and clarify how proposed work complements rather than duplicates existing funded work; address redundancy concerns in application and cover letter if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for transparency and data to justify out-of-order decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for institutes to provide public rationale for out-of-line funding and reference to NIGMS publishing outcome data; 'Now whether NCI should provide a public rationale for why it funded each grant outside the 7% payline is an interesting idea. Send in a FOIA request and see what you get.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect limited public explanation of programmatic exceptions; investigators and observers should consult published institute funding data (e.g., NIGMS graphs) or request information via FOIA when necessary to evaluate fairness or trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between long-term strategic priorities and reviewer conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension exists between peer reviewers (who may be conservative) and Program (which should consider long view, balance of effort, and willingness to take risks): 'We can debate whether a funding agency should be sensitive to the long view...I'll come down squarely in favor of breadth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposing work that is novel/high-risk or fills a strategic gap, emphasize its long-term importance and fit to IC priorities; conversely, recognize that highly innovative proposals may receive conservative peer scores and rely on Program to champion them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of fairness shaped by supply/demand and policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints that the system is 'broken' often reflect supply-demand mismatch and policy changes (e.g., gray zone adjustments) rather than corruption: 'The system is indeed broken. That is because demand for grants greatly outstrips supply... Tight budgets have exacerbated the situation, but this crisis is largely your creation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that perceptions of unfairness frequently arise from structural constraints (budget limits, increasing applicant pool). Manage expectations accordingly and focus on strengthening applications and strategic alignment rather than assuming malicious decision-making.
